newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Chidambaram targets interest rates, prices.
newsitem.headline: India's Chidambaram targets interest rates, prices.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, confident parliament will adopt his pathbreaking budget, has set his sights on cutting interest rates and preventing inflation from throttling economic growth.
Chidambaram told Reuters in an interview on Saturday that prices, credit and foreign exchange inflows will be at the top of the agenda when he meets central bank officials in the capital on Monday.
The meeting comes against the backdrop of strong support in financial circles for the budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year starting on April 1.
Chidambaram presented the tax and spending blueprint last month, and lawmakers are expected to vote on it at the end of April. "I believe the budget will pass," he said.

The budget cut corporate and income tax rates, and sent share prices soaring before profit-taking set in. The near- euphoria, however, has not obscured Chidambaram's concerns over slack bank lending and upward pressure on the rupee and prices.

He sees those trends as potential threats to the budget's aim of spurring economic growth -- which Chidambaram says is the best way to combat poverty. Nearly 36 percent of India's 936 million people live below the poverty line, defined by the government as enough income to buy two meals a day.

Asked to outline his agenda for his meeting with Reserve Bank of India (RBI) officials set to start at 10 a.m. (0430 GMT) on Monday, Chidambaram said he would discuss the need to keep prices stable and to manage a surge in foreign exchange flows.
When Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition assumed power last June, annual inflation as measured by the wholesale price index was below five percent.

More recently, pushed up by an increase in domestic oil prices adopted in July and food price rises, the rate has hovered near eight percent. Analysts say another oil price rise could be in the cards, perhaps next month.

Recent reforms aimed at attracting foreign investment, particularly in ailing infrastructure, and the market-friendly budget have drawn large flows of foreign exchange, putting upward pressure on the rupee.

"Few people realise that there is a downside to these inflows," Chidambaram said. "The upside, of course, is that your foreign exchange reserves appear healthier and healthier. The downside is that it has inflationary consequences."
Chidambaram said the central bank could not be responsible for fixing the exchange rate of the rupee, which on Friday closed at 35.865/870 per U.S. dollar.
But he said the currency could not be allowed to fluctuate wildly, and dismissed a suggestion that it might be pushed down in value to help revive sluggish exports.
To help offset the inflationary impact of large dollar inflows, the government is considering easing restrictions on imports of consumer goods. "It is an option," Chidambaram said.
Chidambaram said he would make it clear to the RBI that credit flows must pick up to ensure adequate industrial growth.
Growth of industrial output slowed to 9.1 percent in April-November 1996 compared to the same period in 1995. The growth rate in April-November 1995 was 11.7 percent.
Bank credit increased only half as much from April 1996 to January 1997 as in the same 10-month period in 1995/96.

"There is still some feeling in the market that adequate credit is not flowing for productive purposes, that interest rates are still high. As a principle I would like interest rates to soften," he said.
